Election Deniers Despair Because Even Donald Trump Isn’t Buying What They’re Selling

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (949 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With his head in his hands, Joe Oltmann cut a dejected figure.
  • But two weeks after the election, nothing had been done.
  • In the wake of the overwhelming victory for the Democrats in the midterm elections, Trump has broadly appeared to accept the results, claiming the losses were the result of his name not appearing on the ballot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With his head in his hands, Joe Oltmann cut a dejected figure. For weeks, the seasoned election denier had promoted the baseless conspiracy theory that the midterms were rigged. He mentioned he had sent the White House a 75-page report laying out in excruciating detail a conspiracy theory about how former Venezuelan officials had infiltrated the US electoral system to rig the outcome in favor of the Democrats. (There is no evidence to support this theory.) He had even, he claimed, spoken on the phone to President Donald Trump.

But two weeks after the election, nothing had been done.

In the wake of the overwhelming victory for the Democrats in the midterm elections, Trump has broadly appeared to accept the results, claiming the losses were the result of his name not appearing on the ballot. While he shared some election conspiracy theories in the days after the election, he’s taken very little action since.

Oltmann is among a group of influential election deniers who believe, without evidence, that the midterms were rigged and who claim to be in direct contact with Trump, but are frustrated by the president’s lack of fervor or seeming interest in overturning the results. These figures are making increasingly desperate demands of the president, including declaring martial law and ordering military tribunals.

Industry observers note that “We can walk into every voting [location] and say: ‘Take this equipment, throw it out in the street,’” states Oltmann. “We can do that … that's not violent … We're just doing our jobs as Americans.”.

These calls for action echo very similar demands made in the weeks leading up to the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, and some of the same figures are involved—though allies in the administration that once boosted their lies appear to have gone silent.

Industry observers note that “This is a carbon copy of 2020,” noted Patrick Byrne, the founder of Overstock.com who claims to have spent $100 million on promoting election integrity over the last six years, on a podcast on Saturday. He also claimed that, two weeks before the attack on the Capitol, he was in a room with Trump advocating for the same measures he is asking Trump to take now.

Industry observers note that the big difference this time around, however, is that, so far, Trump has not been leading the charge. In the weeks after his election loss to former president Joe Biden in 2020, Trump was quick to seize on claims that the election had been rigged. In the lead-up to this year’s midterms, Trump and his administration did everything they could to promote baseless conspiracy theories about noncitizens and mail-in voting; they also weaponized the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice to target those they believed were responsible.

Days after the election this month, as the midterm results rolled in, Trump shared screenshots of X posts from election deniers on his Truth Social account, boosting baseless conspiracy theories about the midterms.

On November 9, he appeared to be ready to embrace those conspiracy theories, writing on Truth Social: “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting “dumps” were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote. It’s all about the machines, which are far more crucial than the voter! President DJT.”.

Election deniers on X and Telegram celebrated, believing that Trump was about to fully endorse their community once again. But in the weeks since, Trump has refrained from posting much of anything about stolen or rigged elections, save for a few limited references.

“I am going to give evidence to the president today … I have a wealth of evidence,” Peter Ticktin, a lawyer and former schoolfriend of Trump, told WIRED in an interview on November 11. Ticktin refused to share the evidence with WIRED and said the documents came from “various sources, some who prefer to be anonymous.”.

Ticktin also remarked he would speak directly to Trump about the complications and would be advocating for the president to “nullify all of the results of the last election and declare martial law.” Ticktin told WIRED on Monday that he had not yet spoken with the president and was hoping to soon. Ticktin appears resigned: “If we take him for what he's saying at this point in time, he's not planning to do anything beyond cooperate with the globalists.”.

While many on the right have followed Trump’s lead in ignoring claims about rigged midterms, a significant number of Republicans believe that the midterm votes were not “free and fair,” according to a new poll from UC San Diego.

In a recent development, major election deniers are split over what to do now. Byrne, for example, disagrees with Oltmann’s suggestion to seize voting machines—but he has another initiative: reinstate Michael Flynn, a prolific election denier, to his former role as Trump’s national security adviser.

Sources indicate that “Instead of going straight to insurrection, [Trump] uses current authorities to go inspect hard drives in 12 cities, and you bring Michael Flynn in as national security adviser, and then turn it over to Michael. Michael can get this all done by December 1,” Byrne said over the weekend. “If you do find foreign activity … then say, OK, I'm nullifying this election, I'm declaring a new election in 120 days.”.

But there is no indication from the administration that anything like this will happen, and Flynn himself has called the election “a master class by the GOP in how to fail.” The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

#2575. Don’t Bring Up AI if You Want to Enjoy Your Thanksgiving

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Don’t Bring Up AI if You Want to Enjoy Your Thanksgiving

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1528 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sophie has never used ChatGPT or Claude.
  • Industry observers note that the reasons behind her firm opposition to AI are multifold.
  • Though her parents and siblings are more or less on the same page, the AI use among her extended family is “pervasive.” She worries her aunt might be “bordering on AI psychosis.” And one of her cousins, a newly introduced mother of twins, created her babies’ “entire feeding and sleeping schedule” using ChatGPT and has invested in an app that uses AI to run pediatric doctor assessments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sophie has never used ChatGPT or Claude. “When I'm Googling, I type in ‘minus AI’ after every single search I do,” indicates the 27-year-old social work student, who lives in North Carolina. “I have deactivated Microsoft Copilot, all the things.”.

Industry observers note that the reasons behind her firm opposition to AI are multifold. She worries about the degradation of critical thinking and cognitive functioning, some AI leaders’ alignment with the Trump administration, and the environmental impact of data centers, particularly on the water supply in nonwhite communities. Her perspective is born of strong ideological convictions: “My anti-AI stance is very deeply ingrained in my anti-capitalist beliefs,” she claims.

Though her parents and siblings are more or less on the same page, the AI use among her extended family is “pervasive.” She worries her aunt might be “bordering on AI psychosis.” And one of her cousins, a newly introduced mother of twins, created her babies’ “entire feeding and sleeping schedule” using ChatGPT and has invested in an app that uses AI to run pediatric doctor assessments.

The stark difference in opinion between Sophie and her relatives can make for some pretty tense family gatherings—something she’s dreading going into Thanksgiving. The topic “comes up every time” they get together. “I’m constantly anticipating frustration and being judged, being told that I am naive,” she says.

AI has been the focus of many an argument in Sophie’s family in recent years. (She and other interviewees chose to use pseudonyms or only first names to prevent further such conflict.) At a family get-together a couple of years ago, Sophie sent her résumé to her family members to get feedback, and the same cousin who uses ChatGPT for her babies’ meal schedule immediately fed the document to ChatGPT. “She didn't ask for my consent to use my intellectual property to train large learning language models,” Sophie says, which started a “huge conflict.” That cousin’s tech founder husband, she adds, asks snarky questions meant to poke holes in her stance, such as “Well, what about if it's a poor Black person in Africa using AI to create wealth for themselves?” And though Sophie successfully convinced a different cousin to stop using ChatGPT, that cousin immediately switched over to Claude, which Sophie describes as “a total white-liberal move to pick the better-branded version of the same evil tool.”.

Recent findings suggest that over the past decade, the US’ chaotic, increasingly polarized political climate has put American families to the test: Trump, immigration, Israel and Palestine, the war in Iran, abortion, and LGBTQ rights are just a few problems that have turned holidays into yelling matches and siblings into strangers. This Thanksgiving, you might want to add AI to the list of topics to avoid bringing up around the table.

It has been revealed that “It's the latest generational beef,” notes Matt Lundquist, a psychologist and the founder and clinical director of Tribeca Therapy in New York City. He has found that arguments over AI are on the rise—especially among families.

Sources indicate that lundquist states the glitch has “created a rupture,” even among people who are normally on the same page. This is the case for Lindsay, a 40-year-old romance novelist in Pennsylvania whose family is “very politically aligned.” Before AI became a hot-button issue, Lindsay says, her family “never had a conversation where you have to be like, ‘Nobody bring up politics. Nobody bring up Israel. Nobody bring up Trump.’” So she was surprised to find herself at odds with her uncle during Passover dinner when he began raving about what he believes are the wonders of ChatGPT.

Industry observers note that as a professional writer, she was upset by her uncle's celebration of AI. Last year, Lindsay found out a book she wrote was used to train AI models. “I was like, ‘Do you understand that ChatGPT is not a magical device? It is being created by pirating work from actual writers.” She tried to convey the message that by using AI, “You're directly harming me.”.

Her uncle was “befuddled” by her reaction and became “giggly and nervous.” This seemed to be the first time he’d heard that AI is trained on the intellectual property of real people left uncredited and uncompensated. “When I'm telling him this, I can see it's really not landing,” she states. “I can tell that he thinks this is a benevolent, harmless thing.”.

Industry observers note that others in creative fields report running into similar arguments with older relatives, particularly those earlier in their careers. For John, a 20-year-old cinematography student in Chicago whose girlfriend works in animation, AI brings up fears around both his own career and the future of art. He claims his dad, a civil and chemical engineer who works in the chemical plant industry, holds AI to a high regard and uses it to offload some of the work of managing plants around the country, organizing data—which makes his job more manageable.

Sources indicate that “It can get heated,” notes John. “I'll say, ‘Oh, this is potentially taking away my job.’ And his response will be like, ‘Well, I don't think that it'll get to that point.’ But then I'll say, ‘Oh, it's already doing that.’” From there, the discussion deteriorates: “Our positions are so ingrained,” he says.

“Folks under 30 are giving their parents shit about some of this stuff,” states Lundquist, who has found that anti-AI sentiment is resonant among young adults, particularly those new to the job market and who haven’t bought a home or raised children. This tracks with research from Pew published in August, which found that a majority of American adults under 30 describe themselves as more concerned than excited about AI—and 73 percent of the same group believe AI will result in fewer jobs. (At the same time, young people are still using AI. Axios reported in August that 61 percent of 18- to 34-year-old respondents to its poll remarked they'd used ChatGPT in the past month, while 48 percent said they’d used Gemini, and 20 percent had used Claude.).

Luke, a 23-year-old living in Toronto, indicates AI has become “the most debated topic in the household by far.” Luke just completed a degree in sports media and is struggling to find an entry-level job. Meanwhile, his dad, who has had a full career in computer science and web development, sees AI “as the next significant step for every single person in the world.”.

It has been revealed that debates over AI are “infecting all of our conversations,” Luke says. Last year, Luke remembers, at Canadian Thanksgiving, “what started off as just a discussion about my career and where I'm going next turned into a discussion about AI.”.

“He wants what's best for me,” Luke says. He assumes his dad worries that taking an anti-AI stance could be “detrimental to my career and making a livelihood.”.

Industry observers note that in the family of Kaleigh, a 26-year-old living in Vermont and working toward a master’s degree in social work, disagreement about AI also falls along this parent-child fault line. The anti-AI stance of her and her younger brother is dismissed by her parents as “a young-person-exclusive take.”.

Recent findings suggest that when Kaleigh last returned to her parents’ house, her mother told her that ChatGPT had helped her redesign their backyard. This upset Kaleigh, as a close friend of hers is working toward a degree in landscape architecture. “It's an art form,” Kaleigh says. “It feels so out of touch or annoying to me to have somebody that has actual money not want to pay somebody to do something creative just because it's easier to access with this data thing.”.

In a recent development, lundquist has found that many older adults are “clueless” about how real the threat of AI feels to younger relatives. “I think if you own your second or third home with a 2.8 percent interest rate and you've already sent your kids to college, you're not worried about this stuff,” he notes. “And so the fact that an AI bot can order your groceries for you is just kind of cool.”.

His advice? Maybe avoid the topic altogether. “If it’s done in the genuine spirit of connection, learning, and exchanging ideas, that’s great,” he notes. “If it’s done in the spirit of ‘This is going to be the 2026 Thanksgiving throwdown,’ that’s probably not very fruitful.”.

If you do decide to go at it, he suggests getting in touch with what you’re actually fighting about. “When people are fighting about things like this, in reality they're probably fighting about other things,” he states. “The real beef is, ‘I’m mad about the pittance you and your generation have left for me. I’m mad about how the world seems to be not rewarding the kinds of things I anticipated it would and the things you anticipated it would as my parents.’”.

Intergenerational fights about AI “hang on a desire to be understood,” he states. “So Dad picking up Claude and asking it for a sweet potato recipe burns in ways that feel like, ‘What the fuck, are you not paying attention?’”.

Your foldable phone deserves better, and Google is making developers deliver

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (491 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Androidcentral

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that google wants Android apps to do more than simply stretch across a bigger screen.
  • Sources indicate that the move adds to the pressure on developers to take foldable phones seriously and not to treat their larger displays as an afterthought.
  • Google's announcement also says those apps must keep important information like scroll positions, text inputs, and media playback when users rotate, resize, fold, or unfold their devices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that google wants Android apps to do more than simply stretch across a bigger screen. Starting in April 2027, developers will have to meet newly introduced adaptive quality standards to keep their apps eligible for publishing and updates on Google Play.

Sources indicate that the move adds to the pressure on developers to take foldable phones seriously and not to treat their larger displays as an afterthought. The newly introduced rules establish Tier 3, or Adaptive Ready, as the minimum requirement for standard apps. That means apps have to use the available screen without letterboxing or compatibility modes.

Google's announcement also says those apps must keep important information like scroll positions, text inputs, and media playback when users rotate, resize, fold, or unfold their devices. Support for multi-window environments is also mandatory.

The tech giant is also working to make store listings do more. Developers may already upload dedicated foldable screenshots in the Play Console, but from April 2027 latest apps and app updates will be required to upload three foldable screenshots, on top of the usual two phone screenshots. These should be of the app running on different foldable screen configurations: square 1:1 inner displays, 4:3 inner displays, and folded outer screens.

In a recent development, apart from basic compatibility, Google has two higher-quality tiers for developers willing to put in extra work. Tier 2, or Adaptive Optimized, includes support for accessories like keyboards, mice, trackpads, and styluses and responsive multi-pane layouts. Tier 1, or Adaptive Differentiated, goes even further, adding support for tabletop and book postures, camera continuity, interactive picture-in-picture, and multiple app instances.

Sources indicate that there’s something for developers in it too. Apps that reach Tier 1 or Tier 2 are eligible for premium Play Store badges, improved merchandising, and editorial features. In essence, Google is trading more visibility for apps that make better use of expensive hardware.

According to recent reports, games have a slightly different timeline and expectations. Foldable screenshots become mandatory in April, and its Tier 3 requirements kick in starting in August 2027. Higher tiers will also consider graphics quality, performance, controller support, and frame-rate stability.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Developers will also have to keep an eye out for another deadline, as new and updated apps must target Android 17’s API level 37 by August 2027. Google also looks to bring its adaptive quality framework to tablets, Googlebooks and Android XR devices.

#2570. Inside the Chinese City Where Furniture Dupes Are Made

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 23m • 📚 Deep Dive (4660 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Inside the Chinese City Where Furniture Dupes Are Made

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4660 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that on the morning of May 31, 2025, Shirley Bekker made an impulsive decision.
  • Industry observers note that two months prior, Bekker had little knowledge of the city of 9 million; she had no idea what hotel to stay at or where to go once she landed.
  • Bekker was in the process of buying her dream one-bedroom apartment in East London and spent weeks obsessively watching home renovation videos on TikTok.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that on the morning of May 31, 2025, Shirley Bekker made an impulsive decision. The then 29-year-old doctor living in London finally pulled the trigger on plane tickets to visit Foshan, in southern China, for a flight later that same day.

Industry observers note that two months prior, Bekker had little knowledge of the city of 9 million; she had no idea what hotel to stay at or where to go once she landed. But Bekker was convinced that six days in Foshan to furnish her apartment—and possibly having all of the furniture shipped back to London—would still be cheaper than getting everything at home. With over 100,000 followers on social media, she also later turned her adventure into content, detailing her finds and their cost.

Bekker was in the process of buying her dream one-bedroom apartment in East London and spent weeks obsessively watching home renovation videos on TikTok. “When I saw that things like a sofa cost thousands of pounds, I was like, ‘OK, I’m convinced now that I’ll probably do something drastic to not have to pay that much,’” she says. Her social media algorithm was already feeding her a radical solution. “Made in China, shit quality?” a Chinese furniture seller said in videos on Bekker’s TikTok feed. “Grass sofa? Our factory has mass-produced it; UFO table? Our factory has mass-produced it.” Soon, Bekker says, her “entire timeline became Foshan, Foshan, Foshan.” She learned all about China’s furniture capital, which each year exports nearly $10 billion worth of couches and beds and bathroom vanities, and everything else you could possibly need for your home.

According to recent reports, bekker is just one of a growing number of people around the world who order furniture directly from factories in Foshan. By either flying to the city—or through WhatsApp, TikTok, AliExpress, or Alibaba—buyers can commission made-to-order pieces. And most importantly, they can purchase dupes.

In 2025, Shirley Bekker flew to China to buy furniture, hoping that even with shipping the cost would be lower than shopping in London.

Duplicates were once primarily the domain of fashion and beauty, but consumers are now seeking out knockoffs of luxury designer furniture that promise the same quality as the original at a much lower cost—even after international shipping rates and tariffs. During the week of April 13, 2025, the number of videos urging Americans to buy directly from Chinese factories soared 250 percent. Tens of thousands of videos had been posted under hashtags like #ChineseFactory, and many of them were about furniture pieces. Some videos garnered millions of views and included contacts of Chinese sellers in the comments.

According to recent reports, @gabwithmeg, a working mom in California, claims on TikTok that she saved at least $100,000 by furnishing her entire house directly from China. “It is all Restoration Hardware and Arhaus-style furniture, and I’m going to tell you exactly how I did it,” she promised her followers in January. @gabwithmeg’s post received over 65,000 likes, and the comments are filled with customers clamoring to opt out of the traditional furniture market, if not bragging about having already done so.

Recent findings suggest that together, they represent a turning tide in furniture shopping for Westerners. If people can buy a couch that looks exactly like the famous Togo for $200 on AliExpress, why would they pay $4,800 for one from Design Within Reach? Sure, Ligne Roset is a legendary brand, famously crafting all its furniture near the French Alps, made by trained artisans using an almost entirely manual process. But not everyone cares about history, owning an original, or the ethics of intellectual property in design. In fact, some furniture buyers, including Bekker, aren’t even aware that some pieces they covet are copies. Bekker feels that designer furniture is more expensive because of the brand name, not necessarily the quality. “Sorry to say, for me, it’s a bit bullshit,” she says. “I’m really not one to buy into the idea that the name of the brand makes it worth the price.”.

Sources indicate that “We’re seeing the beginnings of a revolt against the brandification of everything,” says Christopher Sprigman, a law professor at Fresh York University who has studied the knockoff economy. As a consumer, Sprigman expects brands to offer good and consistent quality, but there is a perception that “there’s no real quality control, there’s no real integrity, it’s basically just advertising and driving up costs, creating demand, creating desire without any real substantial benefit that the consumer can feel or taste or see,” Sprigman says.

The videos Bekker saw never explicitly remarked how much the furniture in Foshan would cost, but she was confident it would be far less than at the posh showrooms in London. Despite not speaking Chinese, she roamed around the furniture markets in Foshan’s warm and humid air. By the end of the trip, she had furnished her entire apartment for around £7,000 (about $9,200). Everything would go in a 20-foot container, embark from Guangzhou on a freight ship, and arrive at an English port more than two months later. Bekker’s videos attracted millions of views, and fans swarmed to the comments with the same refrain: “I have never been so influenced to go to China.”.

Four million people from over 150 countries visit Foshan’s Louvre every year to shop for furniture.

Everyone who goes to Foshan for furniture makes sure to go to the Louvre.

In the central part of Foshan, the Louvre claims to be one of the largest furniture shopping malls in China, and likely the whole world. At over 4 million square feet, it’s bigger than its namesake in France, which is the largest museum in the world; 4 million people from over 150 countries and regions visit Foshan’s Louvre every year to shop for furniture. Past the facade—which looks like an outdated convention center with blue-tinted windows and rows of country flags above the entrance—is an opulent atrium with marble columns and gilded moldings.

Sources indicate that the complex was designed to be part of a tourist experience package, with official certification from the Chinese tourism bureau. There’s a shuttle bus from the nearest international airport and a five-star Sofitel hotel for guests. In addition to tourists from the US and Europe, there are ever more shoppers, architects, and traders from the Middle East, Africa, Russia, Central Asia, and South Asia.

Recent findings suggest that the Louvre contains showrooms for over 2,000 Chinese brands and 400 European ones, so there’s something for everyone. As many of these brands construct their furniture in Foshan, it’s the ideal place for a showroom. Italian minimalism is one of the most visible aesthetics here, but you’ll also find styles like Russian imperial, “upcoming Chinese,” and wabi-sabi. In most places, photography is strictly prohibited to “protect original designs.”.

But the Louvre is often just a shopper’s first destination. “Foshan is not actually one furniture market. It’s a district, it’s a city, it’s an ecosystem,” says Claudia Hofmeister, an Australia-based furniture sourcing agent who has helped clients from around the world buy furniture from Foshan; she has personally traveled there at least six times. While the Louvre is the pinnacle of luxury furniture shopping, Foshan also offers other mid-tier wholesale businesses that are 100 percent Chinese, plus lower-end furniture brands that Hofmeister says she won’t touch. “And there’s a whole lot of other models like major supercenters just dedicated to lighting, tiles, and building supplies,” she says.

Sources indicate that for many travelers, the real shopping doesn’t happen there. The dupe factories, along with home construction and decor manufacturers, are a few miles away in Longjiang. Longjiang is known as the hub of furniture manufacturing, where you can find everything from fabrics to timber to metal parts. Its streets are lined with miles of furniture shops and nothing else. The town has its own exhibition center, but it stands in stark contrast to the opulent tourism spectacle at the Louvre.

The Louvre International Furniture Exhibition Center contains showrooms for over 2,000 Chinese brands and 400 European ones.

In a recent development, every March and August, Longjiang hosts its own furniture fair, which attracts small manufacturers, dealers, and domestic buyers from other parts of China. The furniture brands in the district care less about original design and are sometimes explicit about where they draw inspiration. On the facade of a showroom building next to the exhibition center, a billboard-sized banner advertises a “Lawrence sofa,” a popular 2017 design by the famous Italian brand Minotti that can sell for over $10,000. In their booths, some sellers display portraits of a white “art director,” an Italian flag, or plaster sculptures.

Even for Chinese people, the idea of traveling to Foshan to buy furniture instead of placing orders from home is relatively upcoming. As China’s real estate economy slowed over the past decade, the traditional business model of licensed furniture distribution struggled. Factories now have to contend with tariffs and competition from countries where labor can be cheaper. Sourcing companies position themselves to factories as a more direct connection to consumers. Even though buyers pay to travel, they can save “30 percent to 50 percent” while still gaining access to new designs and high-quality products, says Lin Fangfang, the founder and chairman of Yueanju, one of the earliest and most influential B2C furniture sourcing agents in China.

Recent findings suggest that yueanju, which was founded in 2016, says it has worked closely with the local government to develop the “travel to Foshan” marketing strategy. On the radio nationwide, ads hype shopping for furniture in Foshan, with organized pickups from train stations and airports, as well as customized factory tours based on specific needs and budget. A typical three-day trip costs as little as $170 per person. Agents take care of everything and even provide a cafeteria and nap area with recliners in Yueanju’s office building in Longjiang. “Even though [Longjiang is] only one bridge away, they just won’t come here because they don’t know about us,” Lin says. “[Now], we can accommodate over 200 visitors with no problem on this floor.”.

Services like what Yueanju offers swiftly exploded in popularity, bringing a steady flow of consumers to what had previously been a business-to-business manufacturing hub. They are now working with clients from countries including the US, Russia, Saudi Arabia, and Australia. In March, during Ramadan, the tech giant hosted a group from Saudi Arabia. “They are royals, so their homes are pretty significant,” Lin says. The company customized the shopping experience based on their fasting needs, only going out after 3 pm every day to preserve energy.

Recent findings suggest that the modern history of furniture in Foshan started with a dupe. As the lore goes, in the 1970s a man named Li Jungang working at a carpentry factory got his hands on a couch from nearby Hong Kong, then a British colony. While upholstered furniture took off in Europe in the 17th century, traditional chairs in China were still made of hardwood and had no built-in cushioning. By the 1970s in Hong Kong, upholstered, Western-style couches were all the rage. Li cut open the couch, studied interior construction, and is mentioned to have built what is considered the first-ever upholstered sofa in China. Similar stories citing the origin of Foshan’s relatively short history in modern furniture manufacturing are now proudly recorded in local history books, displayed in furniture showrooms, and retold by every entrepreneur in the city.

The Louvre in Foshan contains showrooms for over 2,000 Chinese brands and 400 European ones.

Italian minimalism is one of the most visible aesthetics at the Louvre, but you’ll also find styles like Russian imperial, “new Chinese,” and wabi-sabi.

According to recent reports, the rest of the story tracks the rise of manufacturing in China. As the government started embracing the market economy in the late 1970s, China became the locus of offshore manufacturing for the rest of the world. Foshan’s voracious entrepreneurs and artisans saw an opportunity to remake the city—which until then was known more for kung fu and local cuisine—into a manufacturing powerhouse. The city became known for factories that specialized in building materials, home appliances, and furniture. Foshan’s home goods industry grew to include over 7,000 businesses that account for at least one-fifth of the furniture market in China. In 2025, Foshan exported $2.65 billion worth of furniture alone. “If you have a home, you have something made in Foshan,” indicates the promotional slogan and industry alliance rolled out by the local government in 2022.

Recent findings suggest that as the city became a furniture juggernaut, it developed an obsession with Italy and, more specifically, Milan, the capital of 20th-century interior design. At Salone del Mobile, the internationally renowned annual furniture fair showcasing some of the most innovative designs in the world, Foshan factory manufacturers study the latest luxury designs from Italian brands. A smaller number of companies bring their own products to the fair, and local furniture leaders also visit to help promote government collaborations between Foshan and Milan. In 2011, a Chinese newspaper reported that during that year’s furniture fair, Fendi Casa refused to admit Chinese visitors to its showroom. (Salone del Mobile did not respond to a request for comment.).

Recent findings suggest that some Foshan furniture makers do copy designs from Salone, and they do it fast. The 2026 fair ended on April 26; by May 11, Foshan furniture factories were posting on Chinese social media about mass-producing the Anywhere sofa by Edra, one of the breakout products of the year. “The first domestic new Anywhere sofa is here,” indicates a Chinese woman in a brightly lit showroom, walking past a sofa that looks identical to the original, on Chinese social media platform Rednote. The account, under the name HY Casa, says it’s a source factory in Foshan that specializes in “high-end Italian minimal made-to-order 1:1 furniture dupes.”.

Recent findings suggest that to create a truly convincing replica, snapping a few photos in Milan is not enough. Wang Xunyong is the owner of EIBA, a furniture brand in Foshan that produces high-end dupes of Minotti sofas by ordering the original, shipping it back to Foshan, and taking it apart to study its internal structure, just like Li did in the ’70s.

A stack of pocket springs at the EIBA factory.

EIBA is a furniture brand in Foshan that produces high-end sofa dupes.

Before the success of EIBA, Wang had a series of failed ventures—restaurants and several other furnishing-related businesses. Eventually, he arrived at a decision: “Instead of doing a hundred mediocre things, it’s better to take one thing to the extreme,” he says in a video posted on his social media account. In 2023, he founded his current company with a small workshop model, leveraging his past experience in the furniture business. This time, it worked.

It has been revealed that wang’s factory in Longjiang occupies the fourth floor of a pristine white industrial building, where a polished lobby opens into a modest showroom/workshop. Several rows of finished sofas sit near the entrance beneath ceiling spotlights. Wang has a makeshift office area that he shares with his sales staff. Every so often, a Bluetooth speaker linked to his phone announces in a flat robotic voice that someone has made a furniture order online. On the workshop floor, five or six women cut and sew sofa fabric, while several men shape foam, spray adhesive, and stretch upholstery over frames.

Industry observers note that wang has never been to Italy. His understanding of Italian design comes from sofas dismantled inside his factory. The first time Wang cut open an Italian-made sofa, he was struck by its complexity. It wasn’t just layers of materials stacked together, but rather a system with different densities, cutting methods, and structural logic working in harmony. He compares the sofa manufacturing process to making a cake: You can standardize the baking process by using a mold, but a complex curve would sometimes require human hands. For a long time, Wang says, many factories focused only on replicating the look of luxury couches. The proportions and silhouettes of the sofas were similar to the originals, but the internal structure was oversimplified. But that misses the essence of what makes a piece of furniture great.

Lin Qi, a factory worker, cuts paper patterns.

Zeng Xiaofeng, a factory worker, cutting fabric.

In a recent development, this path isn’t cheap. Purchasing original pieces requires significant investment, often eight to 10 times the price of the dupes his factory produces. Once the model is thoroughly studied, efficiency improves. Today, Wang notes, his team can complete the reproduction of a new design within 45 days. This methodology has allowed his factory to reach annual sales of 20 million yuan (about $3 million). Unlike Minotti, which makes almost every piece of its custom furniture in Meda, Italy, Chinese factories can count on much lower costs for labor and manufacturing.

To outsiders, Wang’s work is ethically dubious, but he is unapologetic. “What we’re trying to do is copy it first and surpass it later,” he states. “Many people look down on copying others, but we ignore those noises. First, we learn their details and craftsmanship. Once you have the financial strength and vision, you’ll be much better equipped to do your own thing.”.

In his view, as long as a product does not carry the original brand’s logo, it cannot be considered “counterfeit and substandard.” On a more practical level, he has developed strategies to reduce legal risk. Based on his understanding of regulations, Wang says, a piece is legally distinct if there are “seven points of difference,” even if that’s as minor as changing a board’s thickness from 3 centimeters to 2.9.

It has been revealed that wang’s rule of seven is a common belief among Chinese manufacturers, but it’s more folklore than law, says Morgan Pietz, managing partner at the Los Angeles office of Merchant & Gould, who has represented both sides of furniture IP lawsuits. “At least under US law, there’s no rule that if you make seven changes, you are good to go,” he says.

It has been revealed that but it is difficult to legally claim that someone has knocked off a furniture design, lawyers say. In the US, most plaintiffs in the furniture industry need to go down one of two routes: Either they register patents for each of their products, or they need to demonstrate that a layperson would be able to discern the product’s origin. Both are difficult hurdles to clear. Design patents can cost around $5,000, including attorney costs and a filing fee for one product, and they only last 15 years; to make a “trade dress” claim, a furniture organization needs to show that its consumers recognize the design as being from a specific source. In most cases, furniture designs don’t rise to this level of scrutiny. And no matter which route one chooses, bringing the claim to court and enforcing it could cost millions of dollars.

Industry observers note that sometimes there can even be a correlation between the popularity of dupes and the sales of originals, Sprigman says. When studying the luxury fashion knockoff industry in China, he found that buyers of counterfeit handbags can often move on to purchasing the genuine product once they become wealthier. “For some people, you could view dupes as a gateway drug to the traditional thing,” he says.

To Wang, the production of dupes is not only a furniture industry phenomenon but also indicative of how capitalism in China works more broadly. “Many of our industries started from scratch. If you want results as fast as possible, you have to learn from abroad first. Whether it’s equipment, aircraft, artillery, or high-speed rail, haven’t we always followed this same path?”.

International clients select materials at the EIBA furniture factory in Foshan, China.

Recent findings suggest that still, creating dupes is not a business that can scale infinitely. In Wang’s view, the market for copies has become oversaturated, and competitive price wars are eating into profit margins. Foshan brands are now pivoting to original designs, not only out of ethical concerns but also due to market pressure. One day, when he has enough financial capital and experience, he hopes to develop his own designs. And only then will he consider actually traveling to Italy. Not to copy their furniture, but to experience Italian culture and find inspiration.

“You need to truly immerse yourself in that environment to feel what high-end Italian design is really about” he claims.

Almost everything in Nikki Brooks’ new house came from China, which is how she got the nickname “Container Girl.” Brooks, a TikTok influencer in Texas who finds “affordable fashion” for her followers, started looking for furniture for a new home in 2024. In the past two years, she has bought windows, doors, stone countertops, tiles, beds, sofas, and even a golf cart from Chinese manufacturers, enough to fill four shipping containers.

Sources indicate that in addition to her 150,000 followers across TikTok, Instagram, and Facebook, Brooks organized a private Facebook group where over 25,000 members discuss how to source “high-quality, cost-effective materials from overseas—especially China.” In the group, people ask each other how to import, while others share photos of their containers arriving in the US or their beautiful homes stuffed with new purchases. Through affiliate marketing, Brooks also gets commissions from “some” products she recommends, according to her personal website.

“We’ve seen a whole crop of dupe influencers pop up, whose livelihoods are based on helping their audiences find the best deals,” says Sky Canaves, an ecommerce analyst at Emarketer, who spent over a decade reporting on China. According to Canaves, beauty and fashion influencers can take a 10 to 15 percent commission from the sales they encourage; in furniture, which is purchased less frequently, the rate can be around 5 percent, but the cost per item is higher.

While in Foshan, Bekker bought everything she needed for her new apartment.

She decided to shop room by room.

A new generation of consumers—who came of age with Shein, Temu, and Amazon—consult TikTok or Pinterest instead of design magazines and often buy things directly through these apps. They rarely go to stores in person, if at all, and value affordability over virality. (See the Walmart Birkins, fake AirPods Max, Temu celebrity look-alikes, and everything else that’s been duped.).

It has been revealed that “I don’t love the term ‘dupe.’ It sounds awfully cute for something that is essentially buying a knockoff, or a counterfeit, or a theft,” states Coleman Gutshall, the vice president of strategic operations at Bernhardt Design, which develops high-end furniture with designers. From his perspective, an original piece of furniture is more expensive not because of an outrageous margin; Gutshall says his company pays fair wages for over 1,500 employees in North Carolina and works with up-and-coming designers. Many iconic pieces that are duped today were conceived of by innovative designers 50 or 100 years ago, he says, “and in order to keep that continuing, you’ve got to have this constant pipeline of designers. If they can’t make a living through loyalty and through designing, then their talent is going to waste.”.

Recent findings suggest that but not everyone in the design industry is anti-dupe. “There is no way I could ever afford an original, new Togo sofa,” says Lauren Sinclair, an architect in New York. (A real three-seat Togo—the iconic foam-filled modular couch designed by French industrial designer Michel Ducaroy in 1973 and still handmade in France by artisans—sells for about $10,000 today.) In 2022, Sinclair paid a Chinese factory $200, plus another $700 for shipping, to get a sofa that looks just like a Togo but in a custom color and tailored to the exact size of her small New York City living room.

“As an architect, I typically frown on dupes. I know how hard designers work to get a finished product to market and how low the margins are for bespoke furniture design,” says Sinclair, who refrains from using them in her projects. In the case of her personal dupe purchase, she argues it’s ethically acceptable because the design isn’t fresh. “And even if I bought an official, original Togo sofa, would that money ever go to the designer, Michel Ducaroy?” she says. “Definitely not; he died in 2009.”.

Day one would be about the living room; day two was all bedroom; bathrooms, textiles, and decor got their own time too.

On the fourth day, Bekker spent £165 on a fuzzy, round accent chair that she later learned was a copy of a piece designed by Kateryna Sokolova, an indie Ukrainian designer.

Recent findings suggest that from her deep dives on TikTok, Bekker learned about furniture agents. But she knew better: Her mother, who has an international import business and regularly travels to China, told her to always avoid the middlemen. “She had already drilled it into my head from years ago that going with an agent means they’re asking the vendor to add a commission on top every time you are making a transaction,” Bekker claims. Instead, her mom arranged for a Chinese friend to drive her around Foshan on the first day. Beyond that, she had to figure out everything by herself.

Bekker planned her schedule while on her China-bound flight. She decided to shop room by room. Day one would be about the living room; day two was all bedroom; bathrooms, textiles, and decor got their own time too. She posted TikTok videos capturing what she bought: a £350 sofa, a £150 coffee table, a £50 rug, and a £80 solid-wood dining table. Bekker wasn’t explicitly hunting for dupes, but they found a way to her. On the fourth day, she spent £165 on a fuzzy, round accent chair, which she originally thought was over her budget. But the unusually high price prompted Bekker to look up the chair online through a reverse-image search. She discovered it looked exactly like a 2022 chair by Kateryna Sokolova, an indie Ukrainian designer, that sells for over £6,000 in the UK. That pushed her to purchase.

In a recent development, shirley Bekker’s spontaneous furniture shopping trip to Foshan has turned into a side hustle. In July 2025, she began selling a PDF guide of her furniture purchases and their respective seller contacts on Etsy for £12.

In a recent development, ​​In the end, Bekker bought everything she needed for her new apartment, even down to cutlery and bedding (customized with her own logo for an additional £10). She found a warehouse in nearby Guangzhou to store all her purchases before they were shipped to London. As soon as she got home, she started using her lunch breaks to compile a spreadsheet of price comparisons, which Bekker subsequently shared in detail on TikTok: how much each purchase cost her in China and, through reverse-image search, how much a similar item would have cost in the UK.

Bekker’s spontaneous furniture shopping trip was starting to turn into a side hustle. Her followers kept asking how she found suppliers and how they could proposal a trip to Foshan themselves. In July 2025, she began selling a PDF guide of her furniture purchases and their respective seller contacts on Etsy for £12. Five hundred people have bought it since, she says. In September 2025, when Bekker posted a video about receiving the container in London, followers yet again rejoiced. “It’s been MONTHS! So glad this was brought back to me,” one comment reads. Bekker has since returned to Foshan three times, toured more factories, and opened a furniture sourcing agency to plan shopping trips for international clients. The last time she was in Foshan, she ran into a follower whom she had inspired to travel to China to shop for furniture.

#2565. Industry News: Database Leaks Expose 3.5 Billion Usernames, Passwords, and Documents

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (918 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Database Leaks Expose 3.5 Billion Usernames, Passwords, and Documents

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • More than 3.5 billion usernames, passwords, national identity numbers, and documents were left exposed to anyone online in two unrelated databases, according to new findings shared with WIRED.
  • The findings are the latest in a seemingly endless series of revelations about incidents in which inadequately secured data puts people’s personal information at risk.
  • “Personal data is personal data anywhere in the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than 3.5 billion usernames, passwords, national identity numbers, and documents were left exposed to anyone online in two unrelated databases, according to new findings shared with WIRED. The massive troves included data from people in dozens of countries. One seemed focused particularly on Chinese citizens and included more than a billion China-linked records.

The findings are the latest in a seemingly endless series of revelations about incidents in which inadequately secured data puts people’s personal information at risk. But the two examples also provide a window into the scale of current cybercriminal data collection—both information that attackers collect by assembling and organizing other datasets, and troves they amass using info-stealing malware.

“Personal data is personal data anywhere in the world. At this point, personal data for pretty much every American is out there somewhere, and if we look at China or elsewhere, they have the same kinds of problems and security risks,” says Greg Pollock, the director of research at security firm UpGuard, who found one of the exposed databases. “The cybercriminal world is reaping the benefit of decades of bad information security practices.”.

The two exposed databases are unconnected but were found at around the same time by two different researchers. Pollock’s discovery contains more than 1.5 billion aggregated documents and details of predominantly Chinese individuals and businesses. The second trove, found by Black Hills Information Security researcher Jeremiah Fowler, contains around 2 billion login credentials, with hundreds of millions linked to user accounts for mainstream United States tech platforms.

According to recent reports, exposed personal data, including usernames and passwords, has always been instrumental for scammers and cybercriminals. However, as AI cybersecurity capabilities fuel faster vulnerability exploitation, more effective scamming, and ransomware attacks, access to personal data and account credentials can be more key than ever to attackers.

According to recent reports, the data discovered by Pollock includes 1.64 billion documents representing personal information from at least hundreds of millions—if not around a billion—people, most of them seemingly in China based on included national ID numbers. According to his analysis, the unsecured database held at least 840 million “distinct” national ID numbers, 300 million phone numbers, around 11 million student enrollment records, and nearly 8 million business registrations. From a sample of the data, both children and deceased individuals were included in the files, Pollock says.

According to recent reports, the China-linked data sat unauthenticated and openly accessible on the open internet in what seemed to be some sort of cybercriminal or gray market infrastructure. Pollock was unable to trace an owner or find contact information to notify anyone about the exposure, but as he was investigating the leak, the database became inaccessible—seemingly as part of a ransomware attack or some sort of destructive campaign. He indicates the database was actively being updated until the week before he discovered it.

Industry observers note that pollock, who has investigated data privacy and breaches for many years, says that he attempted to validate the data during the time it was accessible, but he can’t be certain about its fidelity or whether the same trove has been circulated elsewhere. It is also possible that it contains duplicate records, though Pollock attempted to check for this. He emphasizes that it seemed like the data had been analyzed carefully for maximum value to its owner.

Sources indicate that “Someone had done some work to bring together a bunch of data and then normalize it to make it useful,” he says. “There’s no legitimate source on Earth that would have all of these things structured in this way, but if you had all of these breaches and brought them together, that would be valuable to an attacker.”.

The larger of the two exposed databases, found by longtime security researcher Jeremiah Fowler, contained around 2 billion credentials and appeared to be data stolen by info-stealer malware, which can collect all login details being used on an infected machine, and collections of other data from potential cybercriminal activity. There is no indication that individual companies or institutions were breached to compile the data, Fowler says.

According to recent reports, “After finding a couple of different repositories for info stealers and malware, I have a search signature to look for them,” Fowler explains to WIRED. “When this popped up, I could not believe just how major it was.”.

In a recent development, fowler says there were 8,471 folders in the exposed database containing plaintext credentials and account details. Some of the folders were named by country, including the US, UK, France, Germany, and dozens more. He found hundreds of millions of mainstream email accounts, tens of millions of .gov, .edu, and .org email addresses, more than 100 million social media accounts, and tens of millions of ecommerce accounts.

Industry observers note that fowler could not determine who owned the database, but he contacted the hosting manufacturer, which removed it from the internet. It’s unclear how long it was online or if anyone else accessed the information.

Sources indicate that the enormous scale of the two exposures could create a sense of hopelessness that individuals are powerless to defend their private information. And there is a public understanding about the extent of data theft across the web. But both researchers point out that after years of this escalating situation, protections like using password managers and enabling multi-factor authentication really have broadly proved effective at keeping attackers out of consumer accounts, even if they aren’t silver bullets against every kind of attack.

Even at full sticker price, picking up a PS5 or PS5 Pro makes a lot of sense if you are upgrading for GTA 6 or catching up on Sony's massive library of current-gen games.

Not since the release of 2014's Level Over headphones has Samsung stepped into the world of over-ear audio devices, and more leaks of its upcoming 'Galaxy Studio' headphones bring us one step closer to its potential unveiling.

We came across a wave of leaks back in October, where we first heard news that Samsung could challenge Sony and Apple with its own flagship headphones, but thanks to the eagle-eyed experts at SammyGuru, we now have illustrations and visual components that showcase the Galaxy Studio's versatile functions.

Sources indicate that from what we know so far, design-wise, the Galaxy Studio headphones come in two shades (black or beige), with collapsible ear pads for travelling. The headphones are also projected to have an 870mAh battery.

Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy Studio headphones have a flexible design. - Samsung is developing high-end Galaxy Studio wireless headphones that may launch with the Galaxy S27 series early next year. - FCC documents suggest the headphones have flexible earcups that fold flat for easier storage and carrying. - They support Bluetooth and Bluetooth LE, will come in Beige and Black, and would be Samsung’s first wireless headphones in over a decade. Visit our website for more in-depth information about this and other Samsung-related news. Source: FCCNovember 5, 2026.

The reigning champion of our best wireless headphones, the Sony WH-1000 XM6 model, has clearly been an influence on the Galaxy Studio's development, but Samsung has also added its own flair to the device.

Just like its competitor, the Galaxy Studio packs most of its controls on the right ear pad. This supports touch gestures that trigger a multitude of functions, including tap to pause and play, double-tap to skip songs, triple-tap to go back, and there's even a touch-and-hold gesture that rolls out an AI assistant. It's pretty standard stuff for headphones, but the AI assistant integration gives it an extra boost.

Sources indicate that as for its audio tools, it's more or less the same story. According to the animations leaked from the outlet, the Galaxy Studio has both Active Noise Canceling (ANC) and Ambient sound modes, with additional controls for ANC level, Ambient sound volume, and noise control level.

Just like Sony's range of over-ear headphones, it's likely that the Galaxy Studio will pack head tracking support, allowing spatial audio to adjust as you move your head. The headphones are expected to have an auto power-off tool where, if no audio is playing, the device turns off after a set period of time. In the APK, Samsung lists options for 30-minute, 60-minute, or 120-minute timeframe settings.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

It has been revealed that on top of this, the left ear pad will sport volume buttons, which Sony's flagship headphones don't have. Instead, you can adjust audio volume by vertically swiping up or down on the left ear pad.

Recent findings suggest that upcoming leak shows Samsung's upcoming wireless headphones, the Galaxy Studio, is a solid AirPods Max and Sony WH-1000XM6 rival - Samsung’s Galaxy Studio headphones reportedly pack an 870mAh battery, USB-C charging, and wired audio playback support. - The leak says they include ANC, ambient sound controls, wear detection, touch gestures, and AI assistant support. - Other features mentioned are 360 Audio with head tracking, Buds Auto Switch, Auracast, Samsung Find, and support for SSC UHQ and LC3 codecs. Visit our website for more in-depth information about this and other Samsung-related news. Source: SammyGuruNovember 19, 2026.

As mentioned, the Galaxy Studio model will mark Samsung's first over-ear headphones release in 12 years, and between then and now, the audio game has changed drastically across the board among tech giants.

Of course, Samsung needs to take a couple of pages from the books of its rivals to play catch-up, but it's also focused on developing its own flagship features — most notably its versatile connectivity.

It has been revealed that in addition to its audio functions, the leaks point to two separate ports (USB-C and 3.5mm), which allow you to connect the Galaxy Studio headphones to a mobile device for wired listening. This is a connectivity feature that Sony has yet to integrate into its own audio hardware lineup.

In a recent development, listening wirelessly via Bluetooth is convenient, but true audiophiles know that wired listening is the best way to bring out the lossless and hi-res quality of digital music streaming. That noted, the leaks don't detail how much the Galaxy Studio headphones reduce latency, the USB audio bit depth, or sample rate, so it'll take a series of hands-on experiences to determine how the headphones perform in that department.

The most frustrating part is that, at the end of the day, the headphones are still in development, so whether or not some of these specs make it into the final product is another story. But if everything lines up according to what we've seen so far, I fear that Sony, Apple, and Bose alike will start shaking in their boots.

Honor just launched its latest smartwatch, the Honor Watch 6 Pro, and it looks like a formidable contender in the wearable space.

Sources indicate that its standout spec is a 1.5-inch AMOLED display capable of delivering a staggering 5,500nits of brightness. This is, as far as I can see per readily available spec information, the brightest smartwatch display on the market right now, beating the 5,000 nits offered by the high-end Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra2 and Garmin fenix 8 Pro.

This should keep it legible in even the harshest sunlight, which every smartwatch user will know can sometimes be a challenge. Despite this brightness, Honor claims that the 515mAh battery will provide up to 18 days of typical usage.

Recent findings suggest that the Honor Watch 6 Pro boasts a 5ATM water resistance (which should make it usable at a depth of up to 50 meters). This is in addition to IP68, IP69, and IP69K dust and water resistance ratings.

You're also getting a wealth of sensors for comprehensive health tracking, including an accelerometer, gyroscope, and optical heart rate sensor, plus dual-frequency GPS for accurate positioning. You can use the watch for contactless payments thanks to its built-in NFC capabilities, too.

All of this comes in an attractive package inspired by premium watchmaking, with a stainless steel front case and nanocrystalline ceramic bezel.

Industry observers note that in my eyes, Honor is one of the most exciting smartphone brands right now. Originally a Huawei subsidiary, the company split off in 2020 and has steadily grown into a serious competitor to the big names like Samsung, Google, Motorola, and Xiaomi. I have tested countless smartphones and tablets, but it's the Honor ones that I keep coming back to because of their high specs and quirky phone designs.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

According to recent reports, honor frequently undercuts its competition with attractive discount coupons and a bombardment of freebies too, and the Honor Watch 6 Pro is no exception. Its price technically starts at £339.99 (that's roughly $450), but the brand is already offering a £100 discount to celebrate the launch, which takes it down to just £229.99 (just above $300).

You also get a free pair of clip-on earbuds, a bonus brown watch strap, and a complimentary 'worry-free' service blueprint that offers one free repair for screen or liquid damage, as well as an extended warranty service (you can read the full terms of that here).

It's a limited-time offer, but I expect it or similar discounts to return regularly in the coming months and, at this price, the value proposition is excellent on paper. It's going head-to-head with the likes of the Samsung Galaxy Watch8 or Huawei Watch Fit 5 Pro, and beats both on battery life and screen brightness.

I also think the design of the Honor Watch 6 Pro is more attractive, as it looks a lot less like a traditional smartwatch than those two alternatives, but that, of course, comes down to personal preference.

It's not a complete slam dunk, though, as Honor loses to Samsung when it comes to availability, as its products are not officially sold in the US. You also have the matter of Honor's MagicOS software, which tends to be less polished than Samsung's One UI Watch in my experience.

I've reached out to Honor to request a unit to see how it stacks up in the real world, so expect a full review soon.

In a recent development, zainab Johnson is a commanding voice in stand-up, known for conversational warmth, sharp storytelling, and a refusal to let anyone box in her perspective. Over 16 years of grinding through open mics in Los Angeles, taping her debut special Hijabs Off, and releasing her Netflix hour Toxically Optimistic, executive produced by Barack and Michelle Obama’s Higher Ground, she has built a reputation for comedy that turns personal stories into universal truths.

In this interview, Johnson sits down with Mashable's Executive Producer, Mark Stetson, to discuss the evolution of her latest hour, Toxically Optimistic, navigating double standards in the industry, and why protecting her artistic process matters more than chasing viral moments.

Johnson looks back on trading a path as a math teacher for Los Angeles open mics, ditching written scripts to find her real voice on stage, and the unforgettable Delta flight attendant job interview that kept her on her comedy path.

Johnson then dives into the craft behind her specials: treating Hijabs Off like a comedy graduation and Toxically Optimistic like a celebration, weaving together her viral opossum bit (Eugene), and challenging the double standards Black and Muslim women face in comedy.

Johnson also addresses the pressure of streaming and social media algorithms: why comics today rush specials too early, why she refused to front-load her Netflix hour, and why nothing replaces experiencing stand-up live in the room.

Zainab Johnson's two hour-long specials are now streaming: Hijabs Off on Prime Video and Toxically Optimistic on Netflix.

Sources indicate that the M5 MacBook Air is the laptop most people should buy, and right now it’s $989, or $310 off its regular $1,299 price. This is the first time the MacBook Air has dropped below $1,000 since the June price hike. This is a fantastic deal for what you get: 16 GB of RAM, 512 GB of storage, and all the other Mac hardware excellence we’ve come to expect.

And while it’s true we may see an M6 refresh in the MacBook Air sometime in the first quarter of 2027, I wouldn’t wait. From my testing of the M6 MacBook Pro, I don’t think it’ll be worth the extra $300 when the M6 MacBook Air eventually lands, especially since we're not expecting anything beyond a minor chip bump this time around. The M5 is still ahead of the competition in performance and can handle heavier workflows and applications than you might assume.

I’ll also note that the larger 15-inch model is on sale right now. It’s down 20 percent to $1,199, which is also a upcoming low for this laptop. The 15-inch MacBook Air is identical to the smaller model in most ways, including display quality, ports, and performance. #2548. Now There’s a GLP-1 in Chocolate Form

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (699 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Now There’s a GLP-1 in Chocolate Form

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (699 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • First came GLP-1 injections, then GLP-1 pills.
  • To be clear, this isn’t a new medication rubber-stamped by the Food and Drug Administration.
  • As GLP-1 shots exploded in popularity, Lilly and Novo Nordisk, which makes Ozempic and Wegovy, knew they could appeal to even more patients if they put their drugs in pill form.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

First came GLP-1 injections, then GLP-1 pills. Now there’s GLP-1 chocolate. That’s right, a GLP-1 drug in chocolate.

To be clear, this isn’t a new medication rubber-stamped by the Food and Drug Administration. It’s a copycat product offered by telehealth outfit Journi Health, and it’s aptly called Melt. The chocolate morsels, which are taken once daily, contain orforglipron, the active ingredient in Eli Lilly’s prescription weight-loss pill Foundayo. (Eli Lilly also makes the GLP-1 injectable medications Mounjaro and Zepbound.).

As GLP-1 shots exploded in popularity, Lilly and Novo Nordisk, which makes Ozempic and Wegovy, knew they could appeal to even more patients if they put their drugs in pill form.

“One of the bigger barriers to adoption has been that some patients just don't want to take an injection,” Ken Custer, executive vice president of Eli Lilly, previously told WIRED. Foundayo was approved in April, while a pill version of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy won approval in December 2025.

And here’s where Journi Health’s pitch comes in. Founder Luna Yu claims Melt is for people who have difficulty with injections or swallowing pills, including those who are newly introduced to GLP-1s as well as those already taking one who are looking to maintain their current weight. “Lastly, it's for the microdosers who are looking for the longevity benefits,” she says. (For the record, taking any GLP-1 medication below the lowest FDA-approved or standard therapeutic dose has not been tested or proven effective in human trials.).

It has been revealed that yu isn’t a doctor, but Melt does require a prescription from one. Would-be patients go through a virtual medical evaluation where a licensed clinician reviews their health history, determines if Melt is a good fit, and sets the dose. It costs $189 for a monthly subscription of 24 individually wrapped squares of chocolate, which includes physician review. (Foundayo’s list price is $649 for a 30-day supply, but with insurance it could be much lower.).

It has been revealed that melt is considered a compounded drug, essentially a custom mix made for a patient by a pharmacy using FDA-approved ingredients but with a formulation that is not itself FDA approved. The FDA allows pharmacies to compound medications when there’s a patient need—for instance, if a patient is allergic to a dye or ingredient in a medication or needs a smaller dose because of their weight—or when the brand-name version is in shortage.

When injectable GLP-1s were in shortage from 2022 through early 2025, compounding pharmacies were allowed to make their own versions for patients, leading to a booming online market. Telehealth companies sold their versions for a fraction of the price of the name-brand medications, making them a more affordable option for people without insurance coverage for GLP-1s.

Now that commercial GLP-1s are no longer in shortage, the FDA indicates pharmacies cannot routinely compound what are “essentially copies” en masse, though there are some exceptions for documented, patient-specific medical needs.

FDA has expressed particular concerns with unapproved GLP-1 drugs and has cracked down on virtual clinics selling them. Eli Lilly has filed multiple lawsuits against companies selling them, but the drugs still remain available online.

When asked about Journi’s Melt, a spokesperson for Eli Lilly told WIRED, “Foundayo is an FDA-approved oral orforglipron medicine, which was developed through years of innovative science and backed by robust clinical trials. An unstudied knockoff that uses chocolate for purported weight loss treats a serious health need as a marketing gimmick. Regulators and law enforcement must take decisive action against knockoff products being marketed to unsuspecting consumers.”.

According to recent reports, yu indicates Journi Health is able to offer Melt because it’s not an exact copy of the original. “It's really in a novel form factor whereby it allows the patient to have a different experience.” Plus, she says, an edible formulation meets a need for patients who have trouble with injections or swallowing pills.

“We've spoken with patients who've discontinued treatment because of these barriers,” she says. “They deserve alternatives worth exploring.”.

Whether the FDA will find this convincing remains to be determined. For now, though, all that stands between patients and the “novel form factor” is a few clicks.

Nathan Fielder teamed with director Lance Oppenheim for the Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything. And as bonkers as this configuration of facts sounds, the resulting three-hour movie is even wilder than you can predict.

Critics are raving. Audiences snapped up tickets to 2,000 showtimes over the opening weekend. And soon, more moviegoers had a chance to see You Can See Everything as distributor A24 expanded its U.S. theatrical release.

It has been revealed that but what if you'd rather ignore the advice from fans saying this movie is a must-see in theaters with a crowd and experience it at home? Or perhaps you just want to know when you can see it again to replay, pause, and freak out on every tiny detail in your own time?

Industry observers note that you Can See Everything is available on digital for rental or purchase as of Nov. 24.

While this falls into A24's usual window from theater to digital release, it's earlier than we expected! But perhaps A24 thought the perfect time to drop one of the most talked about movies of the year was right before the U.S. gathers together over Thanksgiving meals. As you pass the turkey, you can casually ask what your uncle thinks about Billy and that bowl of eggs.

For more on why this release date is surprising, check out Mashable's prior reporting below:.

In terms of speculation, Forbes notes that A24 tends to release titles to digital streaming via premium video-on-demand 31 to 38 days after their theatrical debut. Recent examples using such a streaming strategy include The Drama, The Death of Robin Hood, and Tony.

According to recent reports, however, when an A24 movie is crushing at the box office — as You Can See Everything presently is — that window tends to be longer. For instance, the horror hit Backrooms opened on May 29 and didn't come out until July 14, 46 days later.

Then there's the Oscar campaign question. If You Can See Everything is going to be a contender for the Academy Awards, A24 might keep it off streaming for longer. That strategy would encourage potential voters to see the film in theaters. This not only improves the audience's focus on the film (being less distracted by their phones, for one thing), but also offers viewers the chance to enjoy the community experience of seeing You Can See Everything with a crowd.

Recent findings suggest that last year, when A24 was campaigning Marty Supreme for award season, the studio withheld a digital release for 45 days. However, that movie opened on Christmas Day. So, between You Can See Everything's box office promise, its awards potential, and its fall release date, Fielder fans might have to wait even longer for this title to be available at home if Oscar gold is A24's goal.

But let's say, theoretically, that A24 follows Backrooms or Marty Supreme's digital release proposal. That would mean You Can See Everything would hit digital on Dec. 1.

They support 24-bit/96 kHz UHQ audio when paired with a compatible Samsung Galaxy device. That’s paired with active noise cancellation that adjust to your surroundings in real-time. They also sound good for those on the other end of a call, with Samsung’s Super Clear Call tech reducing noise from your environment, and the blade stem design positioning the microphones closer to your mouth.

Like everything else in Samsung’s product lineup, Galaxy Buds 4 Pro are packed with useful features.

This includes active noise cancellation (ANC) to filter out noise in your surroundings. Samsung even adapts ANC strength to what’s around you, raising the ANC level when you’re somewhere like on a plane, but lowering it when you’re in a quiet park or café. Voice and Siren Detect can automatically switch the earbuds to Ambient mode when you begin a conversation or when an emergency siren is detected.

In a recent development, live Translate offers support for 22 languages to help you have a conversation beyond the language barrier, with speech translated into your ears via Buds 4 Pro and the transcript shown on your phone. Bixby and Gemini are accessible through the earbuds for AI assistance, too. Samsung also offers an FDA-approved hearing aid feature to help amplify sounds around you.

Industry observers note that head gestures allow you to answer or decline calls with a simple shake of your head. Pinch controls manage playback, while swiping adjusts the volume; pinch-and-hold can be customized for supported shortcuts.

No, you don’t have to have a Samsung Galaxy smartphone to use Galaxy Buds 4 Pro.

It has been revealed that because they work over standard Bluetooth, Samsung’s best earbuds work with any smartphone, tablet, and other devices. Galaxy Buds 4 Pro can also connect to Windows PCs as standard Bluetooth audio, although advanced features are more limited outside the Galaxy ecosystem.

It has been revealed that that noted, you’ll get the best experience with Samsung devices. That’s in part because EQ, noise cancellation, and other controls are baked into One UI, but also because Samsung’s best audio codec on Galaxy Buds 4 Pro is proprietary to Galaxy devices. In other words, you’ll get the best sound quality on these earbuds when paired to another Samsung device.

After releasing developer beta 2 of macOS 27.3 earlier this week, the company is now rolling out the public beta for users looking to try the latest features ahead of next month’s official release. Here’s what’s coming.

Last Monday, Apple released macOS 27.3 beta 2, with newly introduced privacy controls for Full Disk Access and automation tools, and the availability of Apple Intelligence in China.

Those came alongside several new features and tools on macOS 27.3 beta 1, including vertical tabs and adaptive dark mode in Safari, native Live Activities support, Markdown rendering in Quick Look, additional checks for potentially harmful content shared through iCloud links, and Siri AI support for Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

And speaking of Siri AI, macOS 27.3 also expands the assistant’s capabilities across Apple’s own apps, allowing users to perform more complex actions in Messages, Music, Calendar, Photos, and Reminders, as well as manage files and folders. Apple is also introducing new tools for third-party developers to build more advanced Siri AI integrations using Markdown-based instructions.

While macOS 27.2 was a rather uneventful enhancement, macOS 27.3 is shaping up to be the biggest update since the release of macOS 27, and people on the public beta can now try out these latest features ahead of their official release.

The release build for macOS 27.3 public beta 2 is 26C5047e, which matches the developer build.

If you’d like to join Apple’s free public beta program, visit beta.apple.com.
